13: And now I will tell you what they told regarding one of the hasidim, to whom they asked what the happiest day of his life was. And he answered: ‘once I was on a ship, with traders that were selling the best types of merchandise, and I went to the lowest part of the ship as to have time alone with the Creator, and there I lay down, in the lowest part. And one of the young merchants saw me, and I was despised in his eyes, and so he began by spitting on me, and took his genitals out and pissed on me, and I was astonished with his boldness! But by God, my soul did not feel hurt by his deeds at all, and once he left I felt a great happiness, that my soul reached such a level of humility, since I became sure that my soul is one of those that actually walk erect, since it worked on itself in this attribute of humility to the point that it did not feel anything at all [from this provocation].’

And our sages, may their memories bring us blessings, said: ‘the ones who merit resurrection are those about whom it is written “awake and sing for joy, you who dwell in the dust” (Isaiah 26:19). It is not stated: You who lie in the dust, but rather: “You who dwell in the dust,” indicating that only one who became a neighbor to the dust in his lifetime will be resurrected” (see Sotah 5a).’ And such a person is one who does not react to being insulted, and about that person it is written: “my victory will stand forever” (Isaiah 51:6).

And even though Isaiah also said “Listen to Me, you who know what’s right, O people who lay My Torah to heart! Fear not mortals’ insults, and be not dismayed at their jeers” (Isaiah 51:7). And even though the text apparently repeats "you who know what’s right, O people who lay My Torah to heart" this is not a repetition, in my view, this is a hint for us to know with whom to talk, those who actually believe in God’s care. And this [also teaches] that if two people are in a dispute in front of a judge, one should not insult his companion, and if it happens the one insulted should be quiet and think that this is actually a good thing, since the disgrace of the insulting part will be revealed to the judge, as well as the malice of their heart. And about this it is written “you who know what’s right”, because such a person believes that God cares, and that God will repay and will answer in the person’s stead, and will give rest to those who really listen, and checks the hearts of people, and knows if their words are really for good or for the opposite. Up to here are his words on our issue.

And with these words we can understand what we say at the end of our tefillah “My God, guard my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit. To those who curse me let my soul be silent and may my soul be like dust to all”. And on the surface it would have been enough to say “let me be silent”, why add the part about the soul? And also the prayer repeats “my soul be like dust”! Rather, the intention is to make us learn that lowliness is impressed in the nature of the soul, so the soul is silent, since it is already possible just to be silent and not return insults, but hatred can be guarded inside one’s heart, as we read “and Esav hated Yaakov, and Esav said in his heart ‘the days of my father’s funeral etc” (Gen. 27:41). And the Text says “a haughty hearted person is an abomination to God” (Prov. 16:5) – even if the haughtiness is only in a person’s heart and does not come out through one’s mouth, and this is why we say “may my soul be silent”, that the soul itself should be silent. And this is the “people who lay My Torah to heart”, that the Yehudah HeHasid z”l explained , and so we explained in the Gate of Love that all haughtiness and anger come only from the side of dross, because the soul, from its nature, is humble in front of God and in front of everything, as Moshe our teacher PBUH said “and we, what [are we]? (Ex. 16:7)
